title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: where the link stands, and what the tag really asks

questions.prompt: "therefore" is an adverb, so it may stand in more than one place inside its clause — but not in every place. In which of these four lines does it sit where English does not allow it?

options.text: The bus was full; therefore, Wassim walked to the market.
The bus was full. Wassim therefore walked to the market.
The bus was full. Wassim, therefore, walked to the market.
The bus was full. Wassim walked therefore to the market.

questions.explanation: "The bus was full. Wassim walked therefore to the market." is the line to cross out: the adverb has been pushed between the verb and what follows it, and English keeps that slot closed. The mistake is a very frequent one, because the linker has been dropped where the ear expects it instead of where the grammar allows it. The three others show the three places English does allow: "The bus was full; therefore, Wassim walked to the market." puts it at the head of the clause, after a semicolon that closes the first one; "The bus was full. Wassim therefore walked to the market." puts it between the subject and the verb, with no commas; and "The bus was full. Wassim, therefore, walked to the market." puts it just after the subject, held between two commas.

questions.prompt: A tag only fits the statement it was built from. Which of these four openings can carry the tag "is he?" at the end?

options.text: Hichem is the new goalkeeper of the team,
Hichem isn't the new goalkeeper,
Hichem was not at the meeting,
Hichem and Rania aren't coming,

questions.explanation: "Hichem isn't the new goalkeeper," is the one: its statement is negative, so the tag must be positive; its auxiliary is is, so is comes back; and its subject is one man, so the pronoun is he. "Hichem is the new goalkeeper of the team," is positive, so its tag turns over the other way and becomes "isn't he?". "Hichem was not at the meeting," is negative and would take a positive tag, but its auxiliary is in the past, so it calls for "was he?". And "Hichem and Rania aren't coming," is negative too, but its subject is two people, so it calls for "are they?".

questions.prompt: Nizar has to ask a shopkeeper he has never met to put a jacket aside for him until Saturday. All four sentences below are correct English. Which one fits the person he is speaking to?

options.text: Put this jacket aside for me until Saturday afternoon, will you?
You will put this jacket aside for me until Saturday.
Could you put this jacket aside for me until Saturday, please?
Let's put this jacket aside until Saturday afternoon.

questions.explanation: "Could you put this jacket aside for me until Saturday, please?" is the one: a bare imperative is perfectly normal between friends, from a teacher to a class, or on a notice, but to a stranger who owes you nothing it lands like an order, and English turns it into a question with could you and please. "Put this jacket aside for me until Saturday afternoon, will you?" softens the order with a tag, which makes it friendly rather than polite — you would say it to a classmate, not to somebody you have never met. "You will put this jacket aside for me until Saturday." uses will as an instruction given from above, the tone of somebody who has authority over the listener. And "Let's put this jacket aside until Saturday afternoon." uses let's, which puts the shopkeeper and Nizar inside the same action, as though they were going to do it together.

questions.prompt: Read this paragraph from a school magazine, then say where its writer stands. "Nobody thinks clearly with an empty stomach: a family that cannot pay for bread and school books has been robbed of half of its choices. Yet I have watched money turn quiet men into hard ones, and I have seen brothers stop speaking over a strip of land. What decides is never the sum in the account; it is the hand that holds it."

options.text: The writer judges money by the use made of it.
The writer believes only the poor can keep their dignity.
The writer is against money in every form.
The writer says money has no effect on people at all.

questions.explanation: "The writer judges money by the use made of it." is where the paragraph lands, and its last sentence says so almost word for word: what decides is not the sum but the hand that holds it. "The writer believes only the poor can keep their dignity." invents a claim the text never makes; it says that money can harden a man, not that poverty makes anybody better. "The writer is against money in every form." ignores the whole first sentence, where the lack of money is described as taking half of a family's choices away. And "The writer says money has no effect on people at all." contradicts the middle of the paragraph, where money hardens men and divides brothers.

questions.prompt: Wassim is halfway to the stadium when he stops and telephones his sister: "You didn't switch off the lights, did you?" She did switch them off before she left. Which answer does English give him?

options.text: No, I did.
Yes, I didn't.
No, I switched them off before I left.
Yes, I did.

questions.explanation: "Yes, I did." is the answer: in English yes and no answer the fact, never the shape of the question. The lights were switched off, so the fact is positive, so the answer opens with yes and repeats the auxiliary of the tag. "No, I did." says no and then states the opposite, so the two halves of the answer fight each other. "Yes, I didn't." makes the same mistake the other way round. And "No, I switched them off before I left." is the trap your own language sets, where a no is used to contradict a negative question; an English ear stops at the no and understands that the lights were left burning.

questions.prompt: The reading of lesson 12 calls money a good servant and a bad master. In which of these four lives has money become the master?

options.text: Nizar puts aside part of his summer wages and buys the bicycle he needs for school.
Rania gives up the studies she loves for the job that pays the most.
Hichem lends a neighbour the fare to the hospital and is paid back in June.
Mouna compares three prices before she buys her books for the year.

questions.explanation: "Rania gives up the studies she loves for the job that pays the most." is the life where money has taken command: the sum decides what she will spend her years doing, and what she wanted is dropped to make room for it. Money is the master when it chooses instead of you. In the three other lives it is still the servant, because in each of them somebody has already decided what the money is for. "Nizar puts aside part of his summer wages and buys the bicycle he needs for school." turns wages into a way of getting to a lesson. "Hichem lends a neighbour the fare to the hospital and is paid back in June." sends the money where a person needed it and takes it back without a quarrel. And "Mouna compares three prices before she buys her books for the year." is the clearest case of all: watching what you spend is holding the reins, not handing them over.
